title: Three times, "read"
hook: the angel presses him and says read, three times, and then the first five verses (96:1–5; Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night in Ramadan: the Night of Power, better than a thousand months, its date kept hidden. Your line was: the night it came. Is your alarm set for a night this week? Day seven hundred twenty-four.

Read. I am not a reader. That exchange happens once in the cave, and then again, and then a third time. In between, the hadith says, the angel takes hold of him and presses him until he can hardly bear it. It's a strange, rough beginning: not a vision of light, but a grip, and a word repeated, and a man saying he can't. Today's word is about the repeating: three times.
screen: `READ. I AM NOT A READER.` → `PRESSED, AND RELEASED.` → `THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. The angel came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave and said: read. He answered, in Arabic, ma ana bi-qari'. The wording reads most naturally as a denial: I am not one who reads, I can't. Some scholars, pointing to other narrations worded differently, also hear a question: what shall I read? Then the angel took hold of him and pressed him hard, released him, and said again: read. The same answer. A second pressing. Read. The same answer. A third pressing. And then the angel didn't ask. He recited. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot." And a few lines on: "Teacheth man that which he knew not." The order matters. The command doesn't come with the ability attached. He says he can't, three times, and the words come anyway, recited to him. Then he carries them home, his heart trembling, the hadith says. Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape: a line heard, said back, heard again, until it stays. And there's a hadith that speaks straight to anyone who finds it hard. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the one who is skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble, honored scribes, and the one who recites it with difficulty, struggling over it, gets a double reward. The struggle counts. Read, and read again.
screen: `MA ANA BI-QARI'.` · `PRESSED, THEN ASKED AGAIN.` · `THE WORDS COME ANYWAY.` · `A DOUBLE REWARD FOR STRUGGLING.` · then, large: `READ, AND READ AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: read something difficult three times. Choose one short passage that's hard for you. A verse, a poem, a paragraph from a book you've been putting off. Read it once, slowly, without trying to understand it all. Breathe. Read it again, and notice one word that catches. Breathe. Read it a third time, and let it stay. If you pray, you can read a verse of the Qur'an, even the line from today: read, in the name of thy Lord. Then sit with what's left. The bell holds the time.
Three times. The angel said read, and the Prophet said I am not a reader, three times, before the first verses of surah ninety-six were given to him. Today's word.
Your line: read, and read again. Today, when something is hard to take in, a page, a message, a verse, go back to it one more time before you give up. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims memorize and learn the Qur'an by repetition, reciting a passage aloud to a teacher again and again until it is held by heart.

fork.setup: you've said you can't, twice, and been pressed hard twice. the voice says read a third time. what happens?
options: you find you can read after all.
you say it again, and the words are given to you.
the angel leaves without a word.
fork.reveal: he answered the same a third time, and then the angel recited: read, in the name of thy Lord. the words came anyway.

original.note: Arabic: his answer in the cave, 'I am not a reader', or 'what shall I read?'

trapdoor: what you thought: the angel told him to read a book.
what it means: a command given three times to a man who said he couldn't, and then the words were given to him.
what a scholar hears: ma ana bi-qari' reads as a denial; other narrations' wording lets some hear a question.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (read; ma ana bi-qari'; pressed three times; the verses; he returned with his heart trembling)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4937 (the skilled reciter with the noble scribes; the one who struggles has a double reward)

notes: The two readings of ma ana bi-qari' (negation vs. interrogative ma) are attributed to 'scholars'; confirm fair and that the hadith leaves it open (some narrations have 'ma aqra'?' or 'kayfa aqra'?').
Index hook says 'the first five verses'; the script quotes 96:1–2 and 96:5 and does not state a count. Year 1 day 86 quoted 96:1–5 in full.
Pickthall 96:1–2 and 96:5 copied from the year-1 script; confirm wording.
Sahih al-Bukhari 4937: confirm number (also Sahih Muslim 798).
Original: confirm vowel marks on مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ.

Editor: 'Muslims learn the Qur'an the way that night began' (a blanket claim) softened to 'Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape'; varied the 'notice' cue and dropped the stock 'that's the line for today' close. Note Bukhari 3 itself recites 96:1–3; the run to 96:5 is in other narrations (e.g. Bukhari 4953); confirm.

Audit: 'both readings have defenders, and the hadith doesn't decide' overstated the case; with the ba', ma ana bi-qari' is grammatically a denial, and the question reading leans on other narrations (ma aqra'?). Teach, myth reveal and trapdoor corrected. 'And it ends' (96:5 is not the end of the surah, and Bukhari 3 stops at 96:3) changed to 'a few lines on'; 'given to him whole' (could imply the whole Qur'an) to 'recited to him'.
